meta.description: Genuine Confucius: Analects Book XV, ch. XXIII. But the exact English is James Legge's 1861 translation of eight Chinese characters, not Confucius's words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Confucius, real source: Analects XV:23. The famous English wording, though, is James Legge's 1861 translation. Verified against the primary text.

answer.label: Spoken by Confucius (as translated by James Legge)
answer.authorDates: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher & philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It is the Analects, Book XV (“Wei Ling Kung”), chapter XXIII: the disciple Tsze-kung asks for a single word to live by, and the Master answers shu — reciprocity. The famous English sentence is James Legge’s translation ↗, first published in 1861, of eight Chinese characters: 己所不欲，勿施於人.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Analects (Lun Yü), Book XV (“Wei Ling Kung”), ch. XXIII
James Legge, in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (London: Trübner & Co., 1861)
己所不欲，勿施於人 (jĭ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén)
Legge prints it as XV:23; the Chinese Text Project and many modern editions number the same passage 15.24

source.excerpt: Tsze-kung asked, saying, ‘Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one’s life?’ The Master said, ‘Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.’
trail: The sentence appears verbatim as BOOK XV, CHAP. XXIII in the Project Gutenberg text of Legge’s translation of the Analects ↗, standing between chapters XXII and XXIV.
The Chinese Text Project ↗ sets the Chinese — 子貢問曰：「有一言而可以終身行之者乎？」子曰：「其恕乎！己所不欲，勿施於人。」 — beside the identical Legge English, and numbers the passage 24 rather than 23.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced Analects material, cited as Chapter XV:23 — not in its Misattributed section, which is where most famous “Confucius” lines end up.

The translation’s date is fixed by the volume itself: the Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ gives Legge, The Chinese Classics, Vol. I, Trübner & Co., 1861, and Wikisource ↗ describes its text as Vol. I of Legge’s Chinese Classics (1861), reprinted in 1893.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Legge’s English text, capitals and all. “Tsze-kung” is Legge’s Victorian romanization of the disciple Zigong — the Chinese Text Project renders the same name “Zi Gong” ↗ alongside the identical Legge translation.

source.rightsNote: The Chinese original has been in the public domain for millennia, and the exact English wording quoted here comes from James Legge’s translation first published in 1861 — long before 1931, so it too is public domain in the United States. That status attaches to Legge’s sentence specifically: a modern translation of the same eight characters is a separate work and may still be in copyright.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher, editor & philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu; also Kongzi, “Master Kong”) was a teacher and sometime official from the state of Lu whose ideas on virtue, ritual, and humane conduct became the backbone of the Confucian tradition. He wrote no book: his words survive in the Analects (Lunyu), which the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes as compiled by first- and second-generation disciples ↗ and then transmitted privately for centuries. Asked here for one word to live by, he gave shu — reciprocity — then defined it in eight characters.

misattribution.heading: Right author, borrowed words
misattribution.intro: The attribution holds — what usually goes wrong here is precision. Confucius is one of the internet’s most-forged authors, and the English sentence everyone shares is a Victorian Scotsman’s prose, not the Master’s.

items.why: The answer in the Analects is eight characters, 己所不欲，勿施於人. “What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others” is Legge’s English ↗ — and Legge rendered the very same eight characters differently elsewhere, giving Analects 12:2 as “not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself” ↗. Quoting the English as Confucius’s exact words overstates the case.

items.who: Commonly merged with the Christian Golden Rule
items.why: The rule most readers know is positive — Matthew 7:12: “all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them” ↗. The Confucian formulation is negative: do not do. The two are routinely quoted as though they were one sentence from one source.

items.who: Confucius, credited with lines he never said
items.why: Wikiquote hands “The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step” back to Laozi’s Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 ↗, and “I hear and I forget…” to Xunzi. Quote Investigator found the Confucius credit for “choose a job you love” “spurious,” first surfacing in a 1985 magazine article ↗. Against that background suspicion is healthy — it just does not survive contact with this passage.

misattribution.truthLine: The verdict: genuinely Confucius, genuinely the Analects — Book XV, ch. XXIII in Legge’s 1861 translation ↗. Just don’t call the English his own words.

context.heading: One word to live by
lead: Tsze-kung wanted a shortcut — a single word he could carry through an entire life. Confucius gave him shu, which Legge set in capitals as RECIPROCITY, then compressed the whole of it into eight characters. The form matters: this is the Golden Rule stated as a restraint rather than a programme. It does not tell you what good to do for people; it tells you to stop short of what you would hate having done to you.

Confucius did not treat it as easy. Earlier in the same collection, at Book V, ch. XI of Legge’s text ↗, Tsze-kung announces that he already lives by the principle — “What I do not wish men to do to me, I also wish not to do to men” — and the Master flatly replies that he has not attained to it. Short enough to memorise in a breath, hard enough to occupy a lifetime: exactly what the disciple asked for.
context.detailsSummary: Why the chapter number keeps moving
detailsBody: XV:23 or 15.24. Legge’s own edition prints this as Book XV, chapter XXIII, and Wikiquote follows him with “Chapter XV:23.” The Chinese Text Project numbers the identical passage 24. Neither is an error — editors have long divided Book XV slightly differently — so citations you meet in the wild read 15:23 or 15:24 for the same eight characters.

The same eight characters, twice. 己所不欲，勿施於人 also appears at Analects 12:2, folded into Confucius’s answer to Chung-kung about perfect virtue. Legge translated it there as “not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself,” which is why the maxim circulates in English in several wordings that are all, underneath, the same sentence.
